a: climbed into a boat on the sea
p: Jesus had asked for a boat to be kept ready (3:9). Now it becomes his pulpit.
b: The crowd presses so hard that Jesus teaches from a boat a little way out, with the people on the slope of the shore. Earlier he told his disciples to keep a small boat ready so the crowd would not crush him (3:9). Water carries sound well, and the coves along the northwest shore between Capernaum and Tabgha slope up from the water like an open-air theater. Tradition has long pointed to one of them as the place of this teaching, though no source fixes the spot. Matthew 13:1–2 tells the same scene more briefly.

p: The Greek parabolē stands for the Hebrew mashal: a proverb, a riddle, a comparison or a short story.
b: A parabolē is literally "something set beside" another thing for comparison. In the Greek Old Testament it renders the Hebrew mashal, which covers proverbs (1 Samuel 24:13), taunts (Isaiah 14:4), riddles (Ezekiel 17:2) and Nathan-style stories. So in Mark a parable can be a one-line picture ("a lamp," 4:21) or a full story (the sower). Mark uses the word for Jesus' sayings already in 3:23, where he answers the scribes "in parables." Chapter 4 is Mark's one long collection of them.

p: The parable opens with "Listen!" and closes with "ears to hear": a call that recalls "Hear, O Israel."
b: Mark frames the sower with the verb "hear" (akouō): "Listen!" (4:3), "ears to hear" (4:9), and the explanation turns on how people "hear the message" (4:15–20). Birger Gerhardsson argued that the parable and its explanation are built on the Shema, Israel's daily confession that begins "Hear, O Israel" (Deuteronomy 6:4–5): the three bad soils fail to love God with heart, soul and strength. Not every scholar accepts the detailed match, but the call to hear rightly is plainly the chapter's theme (4:23–24).

a: one thirty times as much, another sixty, another a hundred
p: Mark counts up (thirty, sixty, a hundred); Matthew counts down. Mark's order ends on the surprise.
b: Matthew 13:8 gives the same yields in the opposite order. Mark's rising order makes the end of the story a crescendo: three failures, then a harvest that keeps growing. A hundredfold recalls Isaac's field when the LORD blessed him (Genesis 26:12). Scholars differ on whether these are real but excellent yields or a deliberate exaggeration; see the note on Matthew 13:8. Either way the parable is about the end: despite loss, God's harvest will be huge.

p: The phrase recalls the prophets' complaint about a people with ears that do not hear.
b: Jeremiah calls Judah a people "who have ears, and they hear nothing" (Jeremiah 5:21), and Ezekiel is told that Israel is a rebellious house with ears that do not hear (Ezekiel 12:2). Moses said the LORD had not yet given Israel "ears to hear" (Deuteronomy 29:4). Jesus' call turns that complaint into an invitation. Mark repeats it at 4:23, and Jesus throws it back at his own disciples in 8:18.

a: the people around him, together with the Twelve
t: A wider circle than the Twelve
p: The insiders are not only the Twelve but everyone who stays around Jesus to ask.
b: Mark separates "the people around him" from "the Twelve" and puts them together. In 3:34 the same phrase, "those around him," named the people Jesus called his mother and brothers, while his own family stood "outside" (3:31–32). So the line between insiders and outsiders is not birth or office but coming close to Jesus and asking. Matthew 13:10 simply says "his disciples."

a: the mystery of the kingdom of God
p: Mark has one "mystery": God's hidden plan, now revealed in Jesus. Matthew and Luke have "mysteries."
b: Mystērion in Jewish Greek does not mean a puzzle but a secret of God's plan that only God can reveal, like the Aramaic raz of Daniel 2:18–19, 27–30. The Dead Sea Scrolls speak the same way of God's "mysteries" made known to the community. Mark's singular suggests one secret: that the kingdom is already arriving, hidden, in Jesus himself. "You have been given" points to God as the giver. See the note on Matthew 13:11. The word is glossed in today's English as God's secret plan, now made known.
r: Daniel 2:18–19; Daniel 2:27–30; Matthew 13:11; Luke 8:10; Romans 16:25–26; Colossians 1:26–27

p: The same word that put Jesus' family "outside" (3:31) now names those who hear only riddles.
b: Mark has just told how Jesus' mother and brothers stood "outside" (exō, 3:31–32) while the crowd sat around him. Now "those outside" are the ones for whom everything stays a parable. Mark seems to mean a position, not a fixed class: the family is outside in chapter 3, yet a disciple can be "hard-hearted" (6:52; 8:17), and a Gentile woman outside Israel understands a parable at once (7:27–29). Being outside is a matter of not drawing near to ask.

p: Mark's Greek says the parables come "so that" outsiders will not see. Interpreters have read the word in four ways.
b: Mark writes hina, normally "in order that," and ends with mēpote, "lest" ("in case"). Readings: (1) purpose: God's judgment works through the parables, as Isaiah's preaching hardened Israel (Isaiah 6:9–10); (2) result: hina as "with the result that" in later Greek; (3) fulfillment: short for a formula saying that Scripture is being fulfilled, as Matthew 13:14 spells out; (4) Joachim Jeremias argued that mēpote reflects an Aramaic word that can mean "unless": unless they turn and are forgiven. Matthew 13:13 changes "so that" to "because." How God's hardening relates to human choice is a question churches answer differently; see the card at Isaiah 6.

p: Isaiah 6:10 ends "and be healed." Mark has "forgiven," as in the Aramaic Targum of Isaiah.
b: Mark's words are a free quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10, not the full text. The Hebrew ends "and turn back, and be healed" (Isaiah 6:10), and the Greek Septuagint "and I would heal them." Mark has "and it be forgiven them," which matches the Targum, the Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah read in synagogues, which also says "forgiven." Many scholars think this shows the saying took shape in an Aramaic-speaking setting. The order is also turned around: Mark puts "look" before "listen."

a: You don't know what this parable means?
p: Here begins one of Mark's main threads: the insiders keep failing to understand.
b: Right after being told they have been given the mystery, the disciples are scolded for not understanding the very first parable. The theme grows: they do not grasp the loaves (6:52), Jesus asks whether they too are still without understanding (7:18), and in 8:17–21 he lists their hardened hearts and unseeing eyes in the words of 4:12. Matthew softens it: "how blessed your eyes are, because they see" (Matthew 13:16). Readers take Mark's harsh portrait as history, as a warning to his own church, or (Theodore Weeden and others) as a polemic against a group that claimed the apostles' authority; most think it is a call to readers to understand where the first disciples did not.

p: Many scholars think the explanation (4:14–20) uses the early church's words; others trace it to Jesus.
b: "The word" (ho logos), used here eight times, is the early church's shorthand for the gospel (Acts 4:31; 8:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:6). Jeremias and many after him argued that the explanation's vocabulary and its turn from the harvest to the soils show the church applying the parable to its own converts. Others, including Gerhardsson and Philip Payne, reply that Jewish parables were often explained, that Jesus naturally spoke of "the word" of God, and that the story and its explanation fit together. Either way, Mark presents it as Jesus' own private teaching.

p: The birds that eat the seed stand for Satan. A Jewish story of the same period tells of evil birds sent to eat seed.
b: In the explanation the birds become Satan, who snatches the word away. Jubilees, a Jewish retelling of Genesis from the 100s BC, tells how Mastema, the chief of the evil spirits, sent ravens and other birds to eat the seed that people sowed, so that they went hungry (Jubilees 11:11–12). Matthew 13:19 says "the evil one," Luke 8:12 "the devil." Mark's Satan has already appeared testing Jesus (1:13) and being bound by the stronger one (3:23–27).

t: A word for a persecuted church
p: Mark's first readers knew persecution. Many date the Gospel after Nero's attack on Rome's Christians in AD 64.
b: "Hardship" (thlipsis) is the word used later for the great distress (13:19, 24), and "persecution" appears again in 10:30. If Mark wrote in Rome after AD 64, his readers had seen believers burned and torn by dogs after the great fire, as Tacitus reports (Annals 15.44), and had seen some fall away. The rocky soil described them exactly: glad at first, then gone when trouble came. Those who place Mark in Syria or Galilee during the Jewish war of AD 66–70 see a similar setting.

p: Apatē means deceit: wealth promises what it cannot give.
b: The phrase is the same as in Matthew 13:22. Apatē is trickery or deceit; the picture is of riches that seem to give safety and in fact choke the word. Mark alone adds "cravings for everything else." The rich man of 10:17–22 is the story version: he goes away grieving, because he owned a great deal (10:22).
orig: ἡ ἀπάτη τοῦ πλούτου (hē apatē tou ploutou)

p: Mark literally says the lamp "comes." Many see a hint at Jesus himself, who has "come."
b: Normally a lamp is "brought" or "lit" (as in Matthew 5:15). Mark's Greek says the lamp "comes" (erchetai). This may be ordinary loose Greek, but Mark often uses "come" of Jesus' mission (1:7, 24, 38; 2:17; 10:45), so many commentators think the lamp is Jesus: hidden for now under parables, but meant to be on the stand for all to see. The definite articles, "the lamp," "the grain basket," "the bed," point to an ordinary one-room house with one lamp.
orig: ἔρχεται ὁ λύχνος (erchetai ho lychnos), 'the lamp comes'

a: There is nothing hidden that is not meant to be shown
p: The secret is not meant to stay secret. Mark's story keeps things hidden until the cross and the empty tomb.
b: This saying answers 4:11–12: parables hide, but only for a time. In Mark, Jesus silences demons (1:34; 3:12) and tells people not to spread his miracles (1:44; 5:43), and after the transfiguration he forbids telling anyone until the Son of Man has risen from the dead (9:9). William Wrede called this the "messianic secret" (1901) and thought Mark created it; others think Jesus really avoided popular messianic labels. Matthew puts the saying in the mission speech (Matthew 10:26), Luke in two places (Luke 8:17; 12:2).

p: A Jewish proverb that Matthew uses about judging others. Mark uses it about hearing.
b: The Mishnah, the Jewish law code compiled about AD 200, states the same rule: "By the measure a person measures, so it is measured to him" (Sotah 1:7). In Matthew it warns against judging: "The measure you use is the one that will be used to measure out to you" (Matthew 7:2). Luke 6:38 applies it to generous giving. In Mark it is about listening: those who give their attention to the message will receive understanding, and more besides.

a: This is how it is with the kingdom of God
p: Matthew and Luke both leave out the seed that grows by itself. No one knows for sure why.
b: The seed growing secretly (4:26–29) is one of the very few passages in Mark that neither Matthew nor Luke uses. Explanations include: they found its point already made by the sower and the mustard seed; its picture of a farmer who just sleeps sounded too passive; or (on the minority view that Mark used Matthew and Luke) Mark added it. Matthew's weeds among the wheat (Matthew 13:24–30), told at the same spot, also has a sleeping farmer and a harvest, and some think it grew from this parable.

a: in a way he himself does not understand
p: The farmer sows and sleeps. The kingdom grows by God's power, not human effort.
b: Readers have taken the farmer's ignorance in several ways. (1) Patience: the kingdom grows by itself, so disciples must not try to force it, perhaps a warning against the Zealots' attempt to bring it by violence. (2) Confidence: small beginnings will surely reach harvest. (3) Some church fathers made the farmer Christ, who sows and then "sleeps" in death, though the farmer's ignorance makes this hard. Ecclesiastes 11:5 says no one knows how life forms in the womb; James 5:7 uses a farmer to teach patience.

p: The Greek automatē, source of "automatic," is the Septuagint's word for what grows by itself in the Sabbath year.
b: Automatē means "of its own accord." In the Greek of Leviticus 25:5 and 25:11 the related word names the crops that come up by themselves in the Sabbath year and the Jubilee, when the land rests and God provides. Some scholars hear that echo: the kingdom's harvest is God's gift, like the grain of the year of release. The word also appears in Acts 12:10, where a prison gate opens "by itself."

p: The words echo Joel's call to swing the sickle because the harvest is ripe, a picture of God's final judgment.
b: Mark's wording is very close to the Greek of Joel 3:13 (4:13 in the Hebrew and Greek numbering), where God calls for the sickle because the harvest is ripe, a picture of the nations judged on the day of the LORD. Revelation 14:14–20 uses the same image for the end. So the quiet parable closes with the end of the age: the kingdom grows hidden, but harvest day will come at God's time.

p: Black mustard grows to about the height of a man in a season. Pliny says once sown it is hard to get rid of.
b: The plant is most likely black mustard, an annual that can reach two or three meters (six to ten feet). Pliny the Elder notes that mustard grows wild and that once it is sown, the ground is hardly ever free of it (Natural History 19.170). The Mishnah's rules on mixing crops treat mustard as a field crop to be kept apart from others (tractate Kilayim). So Jesus compares God's kingdom to a common, spreading, rather weedy plant, not to a stately tree.

a: the tiniest of all the seeds on the earth
p: Orchid seeds are smaller. Jesus uses the mustard seed as the proverbial smallest thing, as Jews of his day did.
b: Some critics object that the mustard seed is not the smallest seed in the world, and some defenders reply that it was the smallest seed farmers in Galilee sowed. Both miss the kind of speech: "as small as a mustard seed" was a proverb. The Mishnah uses it for the smallest amount of blood that counts in purity law (Niddah 5:2), and Jesus uses it for the smallest faith (Matthew 17:20). Mark's Greek even breaks off mid-sentence here, as if the speaker rushes on to the surprise.
orig: μικρότερον ὂν πάντων τῶν σπερμάτων (mikroteron on pantōn tōn spermatōn)

a: the birds of the sky can settle under its shade
p: The Old Testament pictures great empires as trees where all the birds nest. Jesus uses a garden shrub.
b: Daniel 4:12, 21 and Ezekiel 31:6 describe Babylon and Egypt as world-trees where birds nest and beasts shelter; Ezekiel 17:23 promises a cedar planted by God on Israel's mountain where "every bird" will live. Psalm 104:12 has birds singing in the branches. The birds were often read as the nations. Mark's word for "settle" (kataskēnoun) is the word used in the Greek of Daniel 4 (Theodotion's version) and of Psalm 104 (103 in the Greek). Jesus' choice of mustard instead of a cedar may be gentle irony: God's kingdom starts as something small and ordinary, yet it will shelter the nations.
r: Ezekiel 17:22–24; Ezekiel 31:6; Daniel 4:12; Daniel 4:21; Psalm 104:12; Matthew 13:32

a: in the measure they were able to hear
p: Here parables seem to help people understand. In 4:11–12 they seem to hide the truth. Both are true in Mark.
b: Verse 33 sounds kind: Jesus fits his teaching to what his hearers can take in. Verses 11–12 sound severe: parables keep outsiders from seeing. Readers have resolved the tension in different ways: parables reveal to those who want to understand and conceal from those who do not; or the parables' hiddenness is temporary (4:22); or Mark simply holds both, as Isaiah did, that God's word both opens and hardens. Verse 34 adds that the full explanation came privately.

a: Privately, though, he explained everything to his own disciples
p: A pattern in Mark: public sayings, then explanation in private.
b: Mark often has Jesus explain things in private, in a house or apart from the crowd (7:17; 9:28; 10:10; 13:3). The verb "explained" (epelyen) is literally "untied," as one solves a riddle. Mark's readers, who hear the explanations too, are placed among the insiders, but with the warning that the first insiders still misunderstood (4:13).

a: Let's cross over to the far shore
p: The east shore was mostly Gentile country. The lake crossings bind 4:35 to 8:21 together.
b: The far side of the Sea of Galilee, east and southeast, belonged to the Decapolis and to the territory of Philip, where most people were Gentiles. Mark structures this part of his Gospel around boat trips back and forth (4:35; 5:21; 6:45; 8:13), with a storm on the first and the walk on the sea on another. Many read the crossings as a picture of the good news crossing from Jews to Gentiles, ahead of the church's mission.

p: Either without getting ready, or still in the boat he had been teaching from.
b: The Greek phrase "as he was in the boat" can mean that they set off without preparation, or that Jesus was already in the boat he had been teaching from since 4:1 and they simply put out. The second fits the story's setting. Only Mark mentions the "other boats"; they play no further part, which some take as an eyewitness detail and others as a loose end of the tradition.
orig: ὡς ἦν ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ (hōs ēn en tō ploiō)

p: The lake lies about 210 meters below sea level, and winds can drop onto it suddenly from the hills.
b: The Sea of Galilee is a basin ringed by hills, its surface far below sea level. Cooler air pouring down from the Golan heights and the eastern ravines can whip up violent waves with little warning, especially in the afternoon and evening. In 1986 a fishing boat from about the first century was found in the mud near Ginosar; it is about 8 meters (27 feet) long and could hold over a dozen people, giving a good idea of the boat in this story. Mark's lailaps means a squall or whirlwind.

p: Only Mark has it: "the" cushion, perhaps a ballast sack kept in the stern.
b: The proskephalaion is literally a "head-rest." The article suggests a regular piece of the boat's gear. Shelley Wachsmann, who studied the Galilee boat, suggested it was a leather or cloth sack of sand kept in the stern as ballast, a natural place for a tired man to sleep. Matthew and Luke leave out the cushion. Details like this are among the reasons many scholars think Mark is the earliest Gospel, and some, following Papias, that it rests on Peter's memories.

p: Like Jonah asleep in the ship, and like the Psalms' cry, "Why do you sleep, Lord?"
b: Jonah too was asleep below deck in a great storm and was woken by frightened sailors (Jonah 1:4–6). The difference is that Jonah was running from God, while Jesus rests in God (Psalm 4:8; Proverbs 3:24). The disciples' cry also echoes Israel's prayer in a crisis: "Get up! Why do you sleep, Lord?" (Psalm 44:23). In the Psalms it is God who seems asleep and is begged to wake; here it is Jesus.

a: doesn't it matter to you that we are going down?
t: A rebuke Matthew and Luke soften
p: In Mark the disciples accuse Jesus of not caring. Matthew and Luke turn it into a plea.
b: Mark's disciples call Jesus "Teacher" and complain: "doesn't it matter to you?" In Matthew 8:25 they pray, "Lord, save us!" and in Luke 8:24 they cry "Master, master." Most scholars see Matthew and Luke softening Mark's harsher picture of the disciples, which is one strand of the argument that Mark was written first. Those who hold that Mark used Matthew must explain why he would make the disciples ruder.

p: Jesus speaks to the sea with the word he used to silence a demon (1:25).
b: Pephimōso, "be muzzled, be gagged," is the verb Jesus used to silence the unclean spirit in the synagogue (1:25). The Greek verb behind "spoke sternly," epitimaō, is the one Mark uses when Jesus silences demons and commands silence: 1:25 ("gave it a strict order"), 3:12 ("kept giving them strict orders"), 9:25 ("rebuked"), and 8:30, 32, 33 ("rebuked," "rebuke"). The English differs, following Matthew's parallels, but the Greek links them: Mark tells the calming of the sea like an exorcism. In Israel's poetry the raging sea is a power only God can tame: "He brought the gale down to a hush, / and its waves fell silent" (Psalm 107:29; compare Psalm 89:9; Job 38:11).

p: Deiloi means timid, even cowardly. In Mark the opposite of faith is fear.
b: Jesus sets fear and faith against each other, as he will say to Jairus: "Stop being afraid. Just keep believing" (5:36). Deilos is the word for the cowardly in battle (Deuteronomy 20:8 in Greek) and is listed first among those shut out of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:8). "Still" points back over all the disciples have seen. Matthew 8:26 makes it "you with so little faith," his own favorite phrase.

p: The Greek phrase is the one used of Jonah's sailors after the sea went calm.
b: Literally "they feared a great fear." The Greek of Jonah 1:10 and 1:16 uses the same phrase for the sailors, and in 1:16 their fear is fear of the LORD, who has just stilled the sea. The disciples were afraid of the storm; now they are more afraid of the one in the boat. Their question "Who can this be?" is the question Mark wants his readers to answer, and Psalm 107:29 gives the answer: only the LORD stills the sea. The question echoes through the next chapters (6:2–3, 14–16; 8:27–29).

a: They came to the far shore of the sea
p: Jesus lands on the east shore, in the Decapolis, among Gentiles. The pigs show where we are.
b: Everything in this scene marks the place as unclean to a Jewish hearer: Gentile land, tombs, an unclean spirit and a herd of pigs. Jesus has crossed a religious as well as a physical border. Which town is meant is uncertain, because the manuscripts disagree on the name (see the variant on "Gerasenes"). Matthew 8:28 has two men; Mark and Luke have one.

a: a man with an unclean spirit
p: An unclean spirit, a home among the dead, and pigs nearby: three kinds of impurity in one scene.
b: Jewish law treated corpses and graves as the strongest source of impurity (Numbers 19:11–16), pigs as unclean animals (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:8), and Mark calls the demon an "unclean spirit," his usual name for it (1:23). The man is cut off from everyone. Isaiah describes a rebellious people "who sit among the tombs" (Isaiah 65:4) and eat pork in the same verse. Jesus walks straight into all of it, and the uncleanness, not Jesus, is driven out.

a: Nobody was strong enough to tame him
p: No one could bind him; Jesus can. Mark has just told the parable of binding the strong man (3:27).
b: Mark's details pile up: chains, shackles, broken irons, no one "strong enough" (ischyen). In 3:27 Jesus said that no one can plunder the strong man's house unless he first ties up the strong man, and John had announced one stronger than himself (1:7). Here the stronger one meets the strong man's prisoner and sets him free with a word.

p: Many modern readers see severe mental illness. Mark sees a man held by hostile spirits. Readers differ.
b: The man's self-harm, his life among graves and his great strength look to many modern readers like a description of severe mental illness. Mark, like most ancient people, describes it as possession by spirits. Christian readers take different positions: many accept both, that spirits are real and that Mark describes what he saw in his own terms; others read possession as the ancient way to describe illness; Pentecostal and many global Christians see deliverance ministry as continuing today. Mark's point is the same either way: Jesus restores him to his right mind (5:15).

p: The word is proskyneō, which can mean a bow of respect or an act of worship.
b: Proskyneō means to bow low or kneel before someone, as one did before a king; the same word is used for worshiping God. This site translates it "bow down" in Gospel scenes and leaves the reader to see who deserves it. In Mark it appears only here and in 15:19, where soldiers kneel to mock Jesus. A demon, of all beings, gives Jesus the honor due to God's Son, as the spirits did in 3:11.

a: What is there between me and you
t: "What is there between me and you?"
p: A Hebrew way of saying "Leave me alone!" or "What do we have to do with each other?"
b: The phrase copies a Hebrew idiom found in Judges 11:12 and 1 Kings 17:18, used when someone wants to push another away or protest that they have no quarrel. The unclean spirit in the synagogue used the same words (1:24). Matthew 8:29 has the plural, "between us and you." See the note at 1:24.
orig: τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί (ti emoi kai soi)

p: "Most High" is the title of Israel's God most used by or among non-Israelites.
b: "God Most High" (Hebrew El Elyon) is the name Melchizedek uses: "Blessed be Abram by God Most High" (Genesis 14:19). Nebuchadnezzar calls the three Jews "servants of the Most High God" (Daniel 3:26), and the slave girl in Philippi calls Paul's group servants of "the Most High God" (Acts 16:17). The title fits the Gentile setting. The spirit knows what the disciples were still asking in 4:41: who Jesus is.
r: Genesis 14:18–20; Daniel 3:26; Daniel 4:2; Luke 1:32; Luke 8:28; Acts 16:17

a: I put you under oath by God
t: The demon tries an exorcist's spell
p: "I adjure you" was the formula exorcists used on demons. Here a demon uses it on Jesus.
b: Horkizō, "I put you under oath, I adjure," was the standard verb of exorcism and magic. The Jewish exorcists in Acts 19:13 use it, and a Greek magical papyrus from Egypt contains the spell "I adjure you by the god of the Hebrews, Jesus" (Papyri Graecae Magicae IV.3019–20). Here the formula is turned upside down: the spirit tries to bind Jesus by God's name. It fails, because it is Jesus who is giving orders (5:8).
orig: ὁρκίζω σε τὸν θεόν (horkizō se ton theon)

p: In ancient exorcism, knowing a spirit's name was thought to give power over it.
b: Jewish and pagan exorcism stories often have the exorcist force the demon to say its name. The Testament of Solomon, a later Jewish-Christian work outside every Bible, is built around Solomon questioning demons for their names and the angels that defeat them. Jesus' question fits that world, but the answer gives no power over Jesus: the spirits have already tried to use Jesus' own name against him (5:7).

p: A Latin army word. Some read the story as a picture of Roman occupation driven into the sea.
b: Legiōn is a Latin loanword for a Roman army unit of about 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers. For Jews under Roman rule the name was charged. Ched Myers, Gerd Theissen and others read the story politically: the land is "possessed" by Rome, and the unclean horde rushing into the sea recalls Pharaoh's army drowned in the Red Sea (Exodus 14:28; 15:4). Some note that the Tenth Legion, which fought in the Jewish war, had a boar among its emblems. Others think "Legion" simply means "very many" and warn against reading in a political allegory. The text itself says only: "there are a lot of us."

a: not to banish them from the region
p: Ancient people thought spirits belonged to particular places. These ones want to stay put.
b: The spirits beg to stay in the area, as if they were attached to it. In the book of Tobit the demon Asmodeus, driven off by the smell of fish, flees "up into the regions of Egypt" (Tobit 8:3), and the Gospels picture spirits roaming "waterless places" (Matthew 12:43). Luke 8:31 says they begged not to be sent into "the abyss." Mark gives no theory of demons; he shows them pleading and Jesus in command.

t: Pigs and the God of Israel
p: For Jews, pigs were the clearest sign of Gentile life. Under Antiochus, Jews died rather than eat pork.
b: The law forbids eating pork (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:8). When the Syrian king Antiochus IV tried to stamp out Judaism in 167 BC, sacrificing pigs and forcing Jews to eat pork became the test of loyalty (1 Maccabees 1:47; 2 Maccabees 6:18; 7:1). A large herd of pigs therefore tells a Jewish listener this is Gentile country. Many Jewish hearers would have found the end of the herd fitting, even comic: unclean spirits into unclean animals, and both into the sea.
r: Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:8; Isaiah 65:4; Isaiah 66:17; 1 Maccabees 1:47; 2 Maccabees 6:18; Luke 15:15

p: Readers have long asked about the drowned herd and the owners' loss. Answers differ.
b: Readings: (1) The herd's destruction shows the man and the town how many spirits there were and how destructive they were. (2) The demons, not Jesus, destroy the pigs; Jesus only allows them to go. (3) The sea is the home of chaos (4:39), so the spirits go back to the abyss. (4) Critical scholars often see legendary growth or a folk tale of a tricked demon. Moral objections to the farmers' loss go back to ancient critics. The townspeople's reaction (5:17) shows they counted the cost of Jesus' presence.

p: Sōphronounta means sane, self-controlled. Earlier some said Jesus himself was beside himself (3:21).
b: Sōphroneō is the Greek ideal of a sound, balanced mind. The man once naked (Luke 8:27 says so; Mark implies it), shrieking and wounding himself is now sitting, dressed and calm, like a disciple at Jesus' feet. Mark's readers will remember that Jesus' own family said he was "beside himself" (3:21) and the scribes that he had an unclean spirit (3:22, 30). The one accused of madness is the one who brings sanity.

a: And fear took hold of them
p: The town fears the cure more than the madman. Fear runs through Mark to its last verse (16:8).
b: The people were used to the man in the tombs; what frightens them is the power that changed him. Mark keeps showing fear at Jesus' power: the disciples after the storm (4:41), the healed woman (5:33), the disciples on the sea (6:50), and the women at the empty tomb, the last words of the oldest manuscripts (16:8). Such fear can be the beginning of awe, or a reason to send Jesus away, as here.

p: The healed man asks for what the Twelve were chosen for (3:14). Jesus gives him another calling.
b: Jesus appointed the Twelve "to be with him" and to be sent out to preach (3:14). The healed man asks to be with him, using the same phrase. Jesus refuses, not because he rejects him, but because he sends him as the first preacher to the Gentile cities, with the verb Mark uses for the apostles' preaching, kēryssein (5:20, "announcing"; 3:14, "to preach"). A Gentile becomes a missionary before the Twelve are sent (6:7).

p: Elsewhere Jesus orders silence. Here, in Gentile land, he sends the man to tell.
b: Jesus told the cleansed man with skin disease to say nothing (1:44), and he will tell Jairus' household the same (5:43). Here he commands the opposite. Common explanations: in Gentile country there was no danger of stirring up hopes of a political Messiah; or the man is to point to God's mercy, not to a wonder-worker; or Mark is preparing for the Gentile mission. The command fits the pattern of the "messianic secret": the secret is kept where it would mislead, and told where it can be heard.

a: all that the Lord has done for you
p: Jesus says "the Lord" has done this. The man goes and tells what "Jesus" has done.
b: In 5:19 "the Lord" (ho kyrios) means God, the God of Israel who has shown mercy. In 5:20 the man announces what "Jesus" had done. Mark does not comment, but he lets the two lines sit side by side, as he did at the start, where "the way of the Lord" from Isaiah 40:3 is the way Jesus walks (1:2–3). Many scholars see here Mark's quiet way of saying that in Jesus the Lord himself acts.

p: A group of Greek-style cities east of the Jordan, Gerasa and Gadara among them.
b: "Decapolis" means "ten cities." Pliny the Elder lists them (Natural History 5.74), including Scythopolis, Hippos, Gadara, Pella, Philadelphia (modern Amman), Gerasa (modern Jerash) and Damascus, though lists vary. They were Greek in culture, with temples, theaters and a mostly Gentile population, and since Pompey's conquest (63 BC) attached to the Roman province of Syria. Jesus returns to the region in 7:31. The man's preaching makes Gentiles the first wide audience told about Jesus in Mark.

p: The archisynagōgos was a respected layman who ran the synagogue's meetings and building.
b: The title archisynagōgos appears in inscriptions, including the Theodotus inscription from Jerusalem, usually dated before AD 70, which honors a priest and synagogue leader who built a synagogue "for the reading of the law and the teaching of the commandments." A leader arranged the readings and invited speakers (Acts 13:15). That such a man falls at Jesus' feet shows that not all synagogue leaders opposed him; in Mark the conflict is with some scribes and Pharisees, not with Jews as such. Matthew 9:18 calls him simply "an official."

p: The Hebrew name Jair. It may mean "he gives light" or, as some suggest, "he will awaken."
b: Jairus is the Greek form of Jair, the name of a clan leader in Numbers 32:41 and a judge in Judges 10:3–5. The Hebrew is usually explained from or, "light": "he gives light." Some interpreters connect it instead with ur, "wake up," which would fit a story about a girl woken from death, but that sense is uncertain. Mark rarely names people helped by Jesus (Bartimaeus is the other, 10:46); Richard Bauckham argues that such names point to people known in the early church.

a: My little daughter is near the end
p: Mark folds the woman's healing into Jairus' story. The two light up each other.
b: This is one of Mark's "sandwiches" (3:20–35; 6:7–30; 11:12–25; 14:1–11): a story is started, interrupted by another, then finished. The two halves share much: two "daughters" (5:23, 34), twelve years (5:25, 42), fear and faith (5:33–34, 36), touch, and the word "saved" (5:23, 28, 34). A synagogue leader and a nameless, ruined woman both come to Jesus in need. The delay that heals the woman seems to cost the girl her life, until Jesus shows it does not. Matthew 9:18–26 tells both stories far more briefly.

p: The Old Testament has no healing by laying on hands. A Dead Sea Scroll does.
b: In the Old Testament, hands are laid on sacrifices and on people being commissioned (Leviticus 1:4; Numbers 27:18–23), not on the sick. But the Genesis Apocryphon, an Aramaic retelling of Genesis found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, tells how Abram prayed for Pharaoh and laid his hands on his head, and the plague left him (1QapGen 20:28–29). Jesus heals by touch often in Mark (1:31, 41; 6:5; 7:32–33; 8:23–25), and the practice continued in the church (Acts 28:8; James 5:14).

a: a flow of blood twelve years long
p: Leviticus made her ritually unclean. How much that cut her off is debated, and Mark never mentions it.
b: Leviticus 15:25–27 says a woman with a flow of blood outside her monthly period is unclean as long as it lasts, and so is anything she lies or sits on. Ritual impurity was not sin and was common; it mainly barred people from the Temple. Many Christian sermons have pictured her as a total outcast and her touch as defiling Jesus, so that he broke the law to heal her. Amy-Jill Levine and other Jewish scholars point out that Mark never mentions impurity, that nothing in the law forbade her to be in a crowd or to touch someone, and that the contrast of Jesus with a harsh "Judaism" is a later invention. Her suffering in Mark is illness, poverty and failed doctors.

a: Many doctors had put her through a great deal
p: Mark is blunt about the doctors. Luke, by tradition a doctor, softens it, and Matthew leaves it out.
b: Mark says the doctors made her suffer, took all her money and made her worse. Matthew 9:20 drops the line. Luke 8:43 has only that she had spent her living on doctors, and the oldest manuscripts of Luke (P75 and Vaticanus) do not even have that. Ancient remedies for bleeding could be harsh; the Babylonian Talmud records a long list of folk cures for a woman's flow (Shabbat 110a–b). The detail heightens the miracle: what years of treatment could not do, one touch did.

p: People believed power could pass through a healer's clothes. Matthew and Luke say she touched the tassel.
b: Mark says simply "his cloak"; Matthew 9:20 and Luke 8:44 name the tassel, the fringe commanded in Numbers 15:38. Ancient people widely believed a holy person's power could reach others through touch and clothing; Acts tells of Peter's shadow and Paul's handkerchiefs (Acts 5:15; 19:12). Mark does not mock the belief, but Jesus moves it from magic to relationship: he stops, looks for her and names her faith (5:34). Compare 6:56.

p: Mastix means a whip. Mark calls her illness a scourge, as he did in 3:10.
b: Mastix is literally the whip used for flogging; in the Greek Old Testament it is often a "scourge" sent by God (Psalm 32:10; 89:32). Mark uses it for painful diseases (3:10; 5:29, 34). The word does not say God sent this illness, but it shows how it felt: like being beaten for twelve years.

p: Mark speaks of Jesus' power almost physically, and says Jesus did not know who touched him.
b: Mark writes that Jesus felt power (dynamis) leave him and asked who had touched him, then kept looking for her. Matthew 9:22 leaves out both the power going out and the question. Readers have answered in several ways: Jesus truly did not know, sharing human limits (compare 13:32); he knew but asked so that she would come forward and be restored in public; or Mark reports the event as it was remembered. The church fathers usually took the second view; many modern interpreters, Catholic and Protestant, accept the first as part of his real humanity.

a: she told him all the truth
p: Her healing was private. Jesus makes her story public, so that she is restored in front of everyone.
b: She meant to be healed unseen and slip away. Jesus' insistence makes her stand before the crowd, and she tells "all the truth." Many interpreters see this as part of the healing: her twelve-year condition had been known to the town, and now her cure is known too, with Jesus' own word over her. Fear and trembling here are the awe of someone who knows she has been touched by God's power.

p: The only person Jesus calls "daughter" in Mark. She is brought into his family.
b: Jesus has just said that whoever does God's will is his brother and sister and mother (3:35). Now he calls this woman, who has perhaps no family left and certainly no money, "daughter." It also ties her to the story she interrupted: Jairus came about his "little daughter" (5:23), and the messengers will say "Your daughter has died" (5:35).

p: The verb sōzō means both healed and saved. This site keeps "saved" so the double sense shows.
b: She said "I will be saved" (5:28), and Jesus says "your faith has saved you." Sōzō covers rescue from danger, healing from disease and salvation by God. Many translations say "made you well," which is true but hides the link to salvation. Jesus says the same words to blind Bartimaeus (10:52). Mark wants readers to hear both: her body is healed, and she has been made whole before God. See the gloss.
orig: ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε (hē pistis sou sesōken se)

p: A Hebrew farewell and blessing, as Eli said to Hannah.
b: "Go in peace" is a Hebrew blessing (lekhi leshalom), spoken to Hannah by the priest Eli: "Go in peace" (1 Samuel 1:17), and by Jethro to Moses (Exodus 4:18). Shalom means wholeness and well-being, not only calm. Jesus sends the woman off with a blessing and a promise that her healing will last: "be well, rid of your affliction."

p: Parakousas can mean "overhearing" or "refusing to listen." Both fit.
b: Parakouō literally means to hear aside. In the Greek Old Testament and in Matthew 18:17 it means to refuse to listen, to ignore. In other Greek it can mean to overhear. Both make sense: Jesus overheard the message, and he refused to accept its verdict. Many modern translations choose "overhearing"; this site follows the meaning the word has elsewhere in the Bible. Later manuscripts changed it to the plain "hearing" (see the variant).

a: Stop being afraid. Just keep believing.
p: Both commands are in the present tense: stop fearing, go on trusting.
b: Mē phobou is a present command that often means "stop being afraid," and monon pisteue means "only keep on believing." Jairus already had faith enough to come; now he must keep it when the worst news arrives. In Mark fear is the opposite of faith (4:40), and the women at the tomb will end the Gospel afraid (16:8), leaving readers to choose.
orig: μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε (mē phobou, monon pisteue)

a: Peter, James, and John the brother of James
p: First of three times that Jesus takes only Peter, James and John.
b: These three were the first called (1:16–20) and are given new names (3:16–17). They alone will see the transfiguration (9:2) and be taken further into Gethsemane (14:33); Andrew joins them for the discourse on the Mount of Olives (13:3). Each time they witness something about Jesus' identity or suffering that they do not yet understand. Paul later calls Peter, James (by then Jesus' brother, not Zebedee's son) and John the "pillars" in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9).

a: crying and wailing a great deal
p: Jewish mourning was loud and public. Even the poorest family hired flute players and a wailing woman.
b: Mourning began at once after a death, with loud weeping, wailing and often hired help. The Mishnah says that even the poorest man in Israel should provide at least two flutes and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral (Ketubot 4:4). Matthew 9:23 mentions the flute players. The noise means the death is public knowledge, which makes Jesus' order of silence in 5:43 all the more striking.

p: Did Jesus mean she was only in a coma? Most read "sleep" as the Bible's word for death that God will undo.
b: Some rationalist interpreters of the 1800s held that the girl was in a coma and Jesus saw it. But Mark has messengers and mourners declare her dead and has them laugh at Jesus because they know it. "Sleep" is a common Jewish and Christian picture for death as something God will wake people from: "many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake" (Daniel 12:2; compare John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). For Jesus, her death is as easy to end as sleep.

a: Little girl, I tell you, get up
p: Mark keeps Jesus' Aramaic words and translates them for Greek readers.
b: Ṭalyetha is Aramaic for "little girl" (literally "lamb"), and qum is "get up." Aramaic was the everyday language of Jews in Galilee. Mark keeps several of Jesus' Aramaic words and explains them (3:17; 7:11, 34; 14:36; 15:34), which shows he wrote for readers who did not speak it. "I tell you" is Mark's addition to the translation, stressing Jesus' authority. "Get up" (egeire) is the verb used for rising from the dead (16:6).
orig: ταλιθα κουμ (talitha koum), Aramaic ṭalyetha qum

p: The girl had lived twelve years, the woman had suffered twelve. Twelve is also Israel's number.
b: The girl's whole life has lasted as long as the woman's illness. Twelve-year-old girls were on the edge of marriage age in that world, so her death meant the loss of all her future. Twelve is also the number of Israel's tribes and of the disciples (3:14), and some see both women as figures of Israel restored, one after long suffering, one from death. Mark does not explain the number, but he places it on purpose.

a: no one was to find out about this
p: How could a raised girl be kept secret? This is one of the puzzles of Mark's "messianic secret."
b: The mourners knew she was dead; soon the whole town would see her alive. Yet Jesus orders silence. William Wrede (1901) took such commands as Mark's device to explain why Jesus was not recognized as Messiah in his lifetime. Others see real history: Jesus avoided crowds who wanted only a wonder-worker, or wanted time to reach other towns (1:38, 45). Others again read it as narrative irony: the secret cannot be kept (1:45; 7:36). His second order, to feed her, shows she is truly alive and still a child who needs care.

p: Mark does not name the town here, but he has told us Jesus came "from Nazareth of Galilee" (1:9).
b: Patris means one's home town or native land. Nazareth was a small farming village in the hills of lower Galilee, perhaps a few hundred people, about 6 kilometers (4 miles) from the rebuilt city of Sepphoris. It is never mentioned in the Old Testament, in Josephus or in early rabbinic writings, which fits its obscurity (compare John 1:46). Jesus comes with his disciples, as a teacher with a following.

a: Where does he get these things from?
p: The town asks the right question in the wrong spirit. Mark's readers know the answer: from God.
b: The villagers admit the facts: wisdom "given" to him and "acts of power" (dynameis) done through his hands. Their question "where from?" is the question of 4:41 and 6:14–16. The passive "given" hints at the true answer, God. But they think they know where he comes from, his trade and his family (6:3), and that knowledge closes their minds. John's Gospel turns the same irony into a theme (John 7:27–28; 9:29).

p: Men were normally named after their father. Calling Jesus "son of Mary" is unusual, and readers explain it differently.
b: A Jewish man was normally called "son of" his father. Explanations: (1) Joseph had died, so the town named him by his living mother; (2) Mark, who tells no birth story, avoids naming a human father on purpose (compare 1:1, 11); (3) Ethelbert Stauffer and others argued it was a slur suggesting Jesus' birth was irregular; (4) it was simply a way to tell him from other men called Jesus. Harvey McArthur's study found that naming a man after his mother does occur, so the slur theory is not required, though it cannot be ruled out. Matthew 13:55 has "the builder's son," Luke 4:22 "Joseph's son." Some manuscripts read "the son of the builder and of Mary" (see the variant), which removes the bare "son of Mary."
orig: ὁ υἱὸς τῆς Μαρίας (ho huios tēs Marias)

p: Four brothers, named after patriarchs. James later led the Jerusalem church; Judas is linked with the letter of Jude.
b: All four names are old Israelite names (Jacob, Joseph, Judah, Simeon), common among Jews in Jesus' day. James became the leader of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13) and was killed in AD 62 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200). Judas is the Jude to whom the letter of Jude is ascribed (Jude 1). "Joses" is a short form of Joseph; Matthew 13:55 has "Joseph." The sisters are not named; Epiphanius in the 300s gives them as Mary and Salome. Whether these were children of Mary, Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage, or cousins is a question churches answer differently: see the card on this chapter.
r: 3:31–35; 15:40; Matthew 13:55–56; John 7:3–5; Acts 1:14; 1 Corinthians 9:5; Galatians 1:19; Jude 1:1

a: A prophet gets honor everywhere except in his hometown
p: A proverb found in all four Gospels and in the Gospel of Thomas.
b: Jesus quotes a proverb about himself, ranking himself among the prophets. It appears in all the Gospels (Matthew 13:57; Luke 4:24; John 4:44) and in the Gospel of Thomas, a sayings collection outside every Bible, with a second line: "no doctor heals those who know him" (Thomas 31; also on Oxyrhynchus papyrus 1). Mark alone adds "with his relatives," which recalls his family's attempt to seize him (3:21). Jeremiah's own townsmen plotted against him (Jeremiah 11:21).
r: 3:21; Matthew 13:57; Luke 4:24; John 4:44; Jeremiah 11:21; Gospel of Thomas 31

a: He was not able to do any act of power there
p: Mark says Jesus could not. Matthew says he did not do many. Readers have weighed the words carefully.
b: Mark's "could not" is one of the plainest examples of Matthew softening Mark: Matthew 13:58 says "he did not do many acts of power there." Readings: (1) Jesus' acts of power are not magic; they work in a setting of faith, so unbelief really blocked them; (2) "could not" means "would not," since signs given to the unwilling would only harden them (a common view among the fathers); (3) Mark plainly shows Jesus' real human limits. Mark adds at once that he did heal a few people.

p: Elsewhere people are astonished at Jesus. Here he is astonished at them.
b: Thaumazō is usually what crowds do at Jesus (5:20). Only here in Mark is Jesus the one astonished; in Matthew 8:10 he is astonished at a Gentile officer's faith. "Unbelief" (apistia) appears again in 9:24, in a father's cry for help with his unbelief. Mark's picture of a Jesus who can be surprised is part of his frank portrait of Jesus' humanity.
orig: ἐθαύμαζεν διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν (ethaumazen dia tēn apistian)

p: Messengers went in pairs. The law required two witnesses for any testimony.
b: Mark's Greek repeats the number, "two two," a Hebrew way of saying "two by two" (as in Genesis 7:9). Two witnesses were needed to establish any matter in law (Deuteronomy 19:15), and the disciples' "evidence" (6:11) is a kind of testimony. Pairs also gave safety and support. Luke 10:1 sends the seventy-two in pairs; the church sent Barnabas and Saul, Judas and Silas, Paul and Silas (Acts 13:2; 15:27, 40).

p: Mark allows a staff and sandals. Matthew forbids both; Luke forbids the staff.
b: In Mark the Twelve may take a staff and wear sandals (6:9). Matthew 10:10 forbids sandals and a staff; Luke 9:3 forbids a staff. Augustine argued that both are true in different senses: Mark's staff stands for the authority to live on what others give, which Matthew's rule implies (Harmony of the Gospels 2.30). Many modern scholars see different versions of the saying. Mark's list resembles the Passover outfit: "your sandals on your feet, your walking stick in your hand" (Exodus 12:11), a people ready to leave at once.

p: A cloth belt, folded over, served as a purse. Copper was the small change.
b: Men carried money in a long cloth sash, folded over, as in the Greek word zōnē. "Copper" (chalkos) means small coins; Matthew 10:9 lists gold, silver and copper. The disciples are not to carry even small change, or bread or a beggar's bag (pēra), which wandering Cynic philosophers carried. They must depend on the welcome of the towns they visit.

p: The tunic was the long shirt worn under the cloak. A second one was for night or for show.
b: The chitōn was the basic garment, a long shirt worn next to the skin; the himation, the cloak, went over it. People who could afford it kept a spare tunic for warmth at night or for changing. John the Baptist told whoever had two tunics to share with whoever had none (Luke 3:11). The Twelve travel as the poor do.

a: stay there until you move on from there
p: Stay with your first host. Do not shop around for better lodging.
b: Hospitality to travelers was a sacred duty in the Jewish world (Genesis 18:1–8; Job 31:32). Jesus' rule keeps the disciples from moving to a richer house and shaming their first host, and it gives them a base for their work in the town. The early Christian handbook called the Didache, from about AD 100, gives a later version: a traveling apostle should stay one day, or two if needed; if he stays three, he is a false prophet (Didache 11:4–5).
r: Genesis 18:1–8; Job 31:32; Matthew 10:11; Luke 9:4; Luke 10:7; 3 John 1:5–8; Didache 11:4–5

a: shake off the dust beneath your feet
p: A public sign that the town had rejected God's messengers and would answer for it.
b: The gesture says: we take nothing of yours, and the responsibility is now yours. Commentators often compare later rabbinic rules that counted soil from Gentile lands as impure, so the act may treat an unwelcoming Jewish town as if it were foreign soil. Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch, and Paul shook out his clothes at Corinth (Acts 13:51; 18:6). "Evidence to them" (eis martyrion autois) can mean a witness against them or a warning for them.

p: Olive oil was the common medicine of the day. Here it goes with prayer and God's power.
b: Olive oil was used on wounds and for illness (Isaiah 1:6; Luke 10:34), and Josephus says Herod the Great was bathed in oil in his last illness (Jewish War 1.657). Only Mark mentions the Twelve anointing the sick. James 5:14–15 tells church elders to pray over the sick and anoint them with oil in the Lord's name. Churches have drawn different practices from these verses: see the card on this chapter.

p: Antipas was a tetrarch, not a king. His later bid for the title cost him his throne.
b: This is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39 with the Roman title tetrarch, "ruler of a quarter." Matthew 14:1 and Luke 9:7 correctly call him tetrarch. Mark's "king" may be the popular way of speaking, or irony: a man playing king. Josephus tells how Herodias later urged him to ask the emperor Caligula for the title of king, and how instead he was accused and sent into exile in Gaul (Antiquities 18.240–255).

p: Mark sometimes calls John "the one who baptizes" and sometimes "the Baptist." This site keeps the difference.
b: Mark uses the participle ho baptizōn, "the one who baptizes," in 1:4; 6:14 and 6:24, and the noun ho baptistēs, "the Baptist," in 6:25 and 8:28. Matthew always uses the noun. The site renders the first "the Baptizer" and the second "the Baptist," so the reader can see Mark's variation; the meaning is the same.

p: Malachi promised Elijah would come before the day of the LORD. Some thought Jesus was he.
b: Malachi 4:5 promises that God will send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD, and Jews expected his return (Sirach 48:10). The same three opinions, John, Elijah, one of the prophets, come back when Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is (8:28). Mark's own answer is that John was the Elijah who was to come (9:11–13) and Jesus is more than a prophet: the Messiah and God's Son (8:29; 15:39).

a: The John I beheaded: he has been raised!
p: Herod's fear rests on his own crime. Mark uses it to tell John's death and to foreshadow Jesus' own.
b: Herod's words lead into a flashback, the only story in Mark not about Jesus. His idea that John has come back is not a Christian belief in resurrection but a popular fear that a murdered prophet's power could return. Mark's readers hear the irony: it is Jesus, not John, who will be raised from the dead (16:6), and Jesus too will be executed by a ruler who knows he is innocent (15:10–15).

p: Josephus says Herodias' first husband was a half-brother named Herod, not Philip the tetrarch.
b: Josephus says Herodias first married Herod, son of Herod the Great and Mariamne II, who lived as a private citizen; their daughter Salome later married Philip the tetrarch (Antiquities 18.136–137). Antipas then took Herodias, divorcing his first wife, a Nabatean princess, which later brought war. Mark (and Matthew 14:3) calls the first husband Philip. Explanations: the first husband had a double name, "Herod Philip" (an old suggestion with no direct evidence); Mark confused him with Salome's husband; or the tradition simplified a tangled family. Many scholars think Mark is mistaken here; others keep the double-name view.

a: The law does not allow you to have your brother's wife
p: Leviticus forbids marrying a brother's wife. Herodias' first husband was still alive.
b: Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21 forbid a man to marry his brother's wife. The one exception, levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10), applies only when the brother has died without a son, and Herodias had a daughter and a living husband. Josephus too says she broke the laws of her fathers by leaving a living husband (Antiquities 18.136). John spoke as a prophet to a Jewish ruler who claimed to keep the law. Matthew 14:4 has the shorter "to have her."

a: Herodias had it in for John
p: A weak king, a scheming queen and a prophet: the story echoes Ahab, Jezebel and Elijah.
b: Mark's readers know John is Elijah come again (9:13; 1:6 compare 2 Kings 1:8). In Elijah's story the weak King Ahab is ruled by his wife Jezebel, who swears to kill the prophet (1 Kings 19:2) and arranges Naboth's death while Ahab sulks (1 Kings 21). Herodias plays Jezebel's part; she gets what Jezebel failed to get. The echo also prepares for Jesus' saying that they treated John any way they pleased (9:13).

p: Josephus says Herod killed John to stop a possible uprising. Mark tells a story of a grudge and a rash oath.
b: Josephus says Antipas feared that John's great influence over the crowds might lead to revolt, so he struck first, imprisoning him at the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea and executing him there; many Jews saw Herod's later defeat by the Nabateans as God's punishment for it (Antiquities 18.116–119). Mark gives the court story: Herodias' grudge, Herod's respect and fear, and a banquet. The accounts can be read together: political fear on the outside, palace intrigue within. Matthew 14:5 has Herod wanting to kill John but fearing the crowd.

p: Pharaoh's birthday feast ended with the baker's execution. Josephus says Jewish law frowned on birthday drinking feasts.
b: The only other birthday feast in the Bible is Pharaoh's, where he hangs the chief baker (Genesis 40:20–22). Josephus writes that the Jewish law does not allow births to be made an excuse for feasting and heavy drinking (Against Apion 2.204). A Roman-style banquet on the ruler's birthday therefore marks Herod's court as Gentile in its ways. Mark sets it beside Jesus' meal in the wilderness (6:35–44).

p: Mark's guest list suggests Galilee. Josephus says John died at Machaerus, far to the south.
b: The "top officials" (megistanes), the "army commanders" (chiliarchoi, officers over a thousand) and "the first men of Galilee" suggest a feast at Antipas' Galilean capital, Tiberias. Josephus places John's imprisonment and death at Machaerus in Perea (Antiquities 18.119). Antipas ruled both regions, and the Galileans could have traveled, or Mark may not have known the place. Machaerus' excavated palace had dining halls.

p: Mark calls Herodias' daughter korasion, "girl," the same word he used for Jairus' daughter.
b: Josephus names Herodias' daughter Salome (Antiquities 18.136). Mark calls her korasion, "girl" (6:22, 28), the word he used for Jairus' twelve-year-old daughter (5:41–42). A royal girl dancing before a hall of drunken men would have been shocking in that world, and some historians doubt the scene for that reason; others reply that Herod's family did shocking things. Within Mark, the two girls stand side by side: one raised from death and given food, the other used to bring a prophet's head on a platter.

a: even if it is half my kingdom
p: The words of the Persian king to Esther. Antipas had no kingdom of his own to give.
b: Herod borrows a royal phrase from Esther, where the king says, "Even if it is half the kingdom" (Esther 5:3; compare Esther 5:6; 7:2). There it leads to the saving of God's people; here, to the death of God's prophet. The offer is also empty: Antipas ruled at Rome's pleasure and could give away no territory. Mark's readers may hear the irony of a "king" (6:14) promising what he does not own.

p: At Herod's banquet the last course is a prophet's head. Jesus' banquet follows at once.
b: The pinax was a flat serving dish. The detail turns the prophet's head into a grisly course of the meal. Mark sets this feast of the powerful, where a prophet dies, right before the meal in the wilderness, where the poor are fed (6:35–44). One banquet takes life, the other gives it. Christian art, from medieval altarpieces to Caravaggio and Oscar Wilde's play Salome, has kept the platter in memory.

a: with his oaths and his table guests in mind
p: Herod keeps a sinful oath to save face. Jewish teachers allowed such vows to be undone.
b: Herod could have broken an oath to do murder; the law treats a rash oath as something to confess, not to carry out (Leviticus 5:4–6), and later rabbis developed ways to release a person from vows (Mishnah, tractate Nedarim). Jephthah's vow is the Bible's warning example (Judges 11:30–40). Herod is "grieved" (perilypos), the word Jesus uses of himself in Gethsemane (14:34), but he values his honor before his guests more than a righteous man's life.

p: Spekoulatōr is the Latin speculator, a guard or scout who also carried out executions.
b: Spekoulatōr is borrowed from Latin speculator, originally a scout, then a member of a commander's bodyguard who also carried out death sentences. It is one of several Latin words in Mark ("legion," 5:9; "denarius," 6:37; the "centurion," 15:39), which some take as a sign that Mark wrote for readers in Rome, though Latin army words were used all over the eastern empire.

p: John's disciples bury their teacher. Jesus' disciples will flee, and a stranger will bury him (15:43–46).
b: The story of John ends with burial, just as Jesus' story will (15:42–47). John's disciples come, take the corpse and lay it in a tomb. When Jesus dies, his disciples have scattered (14:50), and it is Joseph of Arimathea who lays him in a tomb. Mark's readers are invited to compare: John was "Elijah" who came first (9:11–13), and they treated him any way they pleased (9:13), as they will treat the Son of Man.

p: The only place Mark calls the Twelve "apostles": men sent out, now back to report.
b: Apostolos means "one who is sent." Mark uses the noun only here (some manuscripts also have it at 3:14), right after the Twelve return from being sent (6:7). So the word may still have its plain sense, "the ones who were sent." In Luke and Acts it becomes the regular title for the Twelve. Their report of "all they had done and all they had taught" frames the story of John's death, the second half of Mark's sandwich (6:7–13, 30).

p: Erēmos topos: a deserted place, the word of Israel's wilderness and of John's preaching.
b: Erēmos is the "wilderness" where John preached and Jesus was tested (1:3–4, 12–13), and where Jesus went to pray (1:35, 45). Here it prepares for the feeding: as God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16; the psalm asks, "Is God able to lay out a table in the wilderness?" Psalm 78:19), Jesus will feed the crowd in a wilderness place. The disciples themselves repeat the word in 6:35.

p: Around the north end of the lake, people walking could arrive before a boat working against the wind.
b: A boat crossing the north part of the lake covers only a few miles, and with a head wind it moves slowly. A crowd walking around the shore from Capernaum toward Bethsaida could reach a landing place first. Luke 9:10 places the feeding near Bethsaida. Mark's picture is of people so eager that they outrun the boat.

a: like sheep that have no shepherd
p: Moses' prayer for a leader, Micaiah's vision, Ezekiel's promise: Israel without a true shepherd.
b: Moses asked God for a leader so that the people would not be "like sheep with no one to shepherd them" (Numbers 27:17), and God gave Joshua, whose Greek name is "Jesus." Micaiah saw Israel scattered "like a flock with no shepherd" (1 Kings 22:17). Ezekiel 34 condemns Israel's bad shepherds and promises that God himself will shepherd his flock, and set his servant David over them. Jesus' first act as shepherd is to teach; then he feeds them in green pasture (6:39; Psalm 23:2).
r: Numbers 27:15–18; 1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5; Ezekiel 34:11–15; Ezekiel 34:23; Zechariah 10:2; Matthew 9:36; John 10:11

p: Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves and had food left over. Jesus feeds thousands.
b: In 2 Kings 4:42–44, a man brings Elisha twenty barley loaves. Elisha says, "Let the people have it to eat" (2 Kings 4:43), his servant objects that it is not enough for a hundred men, they eat, "and there was extra." Mark's story follows the same pattern: a command to give food, a protest, an amount too small, a meal with leftovers. The emphatic "you yourselves" also gives the disciples a share in the work.
r: 2 Kings 4:42–44; Numbers 11:13; Numbers 11:22; Matthew 14:16; Luke 9:13; John 6:5–9

p: A denarius was a day's pay for a laborer. Two hundred was a fortune for poor fishermen.
b: The denarius was a Roman silver coin, the usual daily wage for a farm worker; in Jesus' parable the owner agrees with the workers on "one denarius for the day's work" (Matthew 20:2). Two hundred denarii is two hundred days' work, roughly eight months' pay for a laborer, since no one was paid on Sabbaths and feast days. The disciples' question points out how impossible the order is. John 6:7 gives the same figure.

p: Symposia means drinking parties or dinner groups. Jesus seats the crowd like guests at a banquet.
b: Mark repeats the word, symposia symposia, a Hebrew-style way of saying "group by group." A symposion was a Greek dinner or drinking party where guests reclined. Herod has just held a real banquet (6:21); now Jesus has the poor recline as guests at a banquet of his own. Some see a foretaste of the feast of the age to come (Isaiah 25:6).

p: Grass is green in Galilee only in spring, near Passover. The scene also echoes Psalm 23.
b: Only Mark mentions that the grass was green. In Galilee grass is green after the winter rains, roughly February to April, which fits John's note that Passover was near (John 6:4, 10). The shepherd who has the flock "lie down" (Mark's word is "recline") on green grass recalls the psalm: "In meadows of fresh grass he has me lie down" (Psalm 23:2). Details like this are part of the argument for an eyewitness source behind Mark.

p: Moses organized Israel in thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Mark's crowd is arranged like Israel in the wilderness.
b: On Jethro's advice, Moses set leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (Exodus 18:21, 25). The Dead Sea community arranged itself the same way, as the true Israel of the end time (Community Rule 2:21–22; Damascus Document 13:1–2). Mark's crowd sits in groups of hundreds and fifties: a new Israel gathered in the wilderness and fed by God. The word for the groups, prasiai, means garden beds, picturing the neat rows of people on the grass.
orig: πρασιαὶ πρασιαί (prasiai prasiai), 'garden bed by garden bed'
r: Exodus 18:21; Exodus 18:25; Deuteronomy 1:15; Community Rule 2:21–22; Damascus Document 13:1–2

p: A Jewish host blessed God before breaking bread. The blessing is to God, not over the bread.
b: Jewish custom, recorded in the Mishnah, had the head of the meal say a blessing to God before eating bread: "Blessed are you ... who brings forth bread from the earth" (Berakhot 6:1). Jesus acts as host. Looking up to heaven, a gesture of prayer (7:34; John 11:41; 17:1), shows to whom the blessing goes. The same words, took, blessed, broke, gave, describe the second feeding (8:6) and the Last Supper (14:22).

a: He broke the loaves and kept handing them to his disciples
p: Took, blessed, broke, gave: the four actions of the Lord's Supper (14:22).
b: At the Last Supper Jesus takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it (14:22). The early church, which met to "break bread" (Acts 2:42), heard the feedings with those words in mind. Mark makes the disciples the servers who hand out what Jesus gives, as church leaders later served at the table. The fathers read the feeding as a sign of the Eucharist; many modern scholars agree Mark shaped it that way, while noting that fish, not wine, is shared here.

p: Twelve, as in the tribes of Israel and the Twelve who served. The basket was a typically Jewish one.
b: Twelve baskets, perhaps one for each of the Twelve; and twelve recalls the tribes of Israel. Mark's word kophinos was associated with Jews: the Roman poet Juvenal mocks Jews whose belongings were a basket and hay (Satires 3.14; 6.542). At the feeding of the four thousand the baskets are seven, a different word (spyris, 8:8). Jesus later asks the disciples to count both (8:19–20), as if the numbers mean something they have missed.

a: The men who ate the loaves
p: The Greek andres means males. Matthew adds "apart from women and children."
b: Mark uses andres, men as opposed to women, not the general word for people. Counting men was normal in Jewish reckoning (Exodus 12:37). Matthew 14:21 adds "apart from women and children," so the full crowd was larger. Some scholars see a gathering of men around a hoped-for leader, as John 6:15 says the crowd wanted to make Jesus king. Mark does not say so.

p: The disciples set off for Bethsaida but land at Gennesaret (6:53). Readers explain the change differently.
b: Bethsaida, "house of fishing," lay near where the Jordan enters the lake from the north; archaeologists debate whether it is et-Tell or el-Araj. The disciples head there but come ashore at Gennesaret on the west side (6:53), and reach Bethsaida only in 8:22. Explanations: the head wind drove them off course; "to the far shore, toward Bethsaida" means a short hop along the north coast; or Mark joined separate stories. Mark may also mean the disciples do not arrive until they understand (8:21–22).

p: Mark shows Jesus praying alone three times, each at night and at a turning point.
b: Mark records Jesus praying alone in the early morning after his first day of healing (1:35), here at night after the feeding, and in Gethsemane before his arrest (14:32–39). Each follows a moment when crowds want him for the wrong reasons, and each is followed by a moment when the disciples fail him. John 6:15 says that after the feeding the crowd wanted to make him king by force.

p: Romans divided the night into four watches. The fourth ran from about 3 to 6 a.m.
b: Jews traditionally counted three night watches (Judges 7:19), but Roman custom, used in Mark and Matthew, had four: evening, midnight, cockcrow and early morning, the names Jesus uses in 13:35. The fourth watch is the last stretch before dawn. The disciples have been rowing since evening (6:47), most of the night. Jesus comes when they are worn out.

p: In the Old Testament only God walks on the sea.
b: Job says of God, "Alone he spreads out the skies / and tramples on the back of the Sea" (Job 9:8), and the Psalms say of the Exodus, "Your road was in the sea" (Psalm 77:19). Isaiah promises a way through the waters for God's people (Isaiah 43:16). Mark tells the story so that a Jewish reader hears God's own acts. Some critics read it as a story of a vision, or as a resurrection appearance moved back into Jesus' life; believers read it as a miracle that shows who Jesus is.
r: Job 9:8; Job 38:16; Psalm 77:19; Isaiah 43:16; Matthew 14:25; John 6:19

a: He was intending to go past them
p: Why go past them? In Exodus, God "passes by" to show his glory to Moses and Elijah.
b: The phrase is puzzling if it means Jesus would ignore his struggling disciples. But "pass by" (parerchomai) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses when God reveals himself: "The LORD passed in front of him" (Exodus 34:6; compare Exodus 33:19, 22), and to Elijah, "look: the LORD was passing by" (1 Kings 19:11). Job says of God, "He could walk right past me and I would not see" (Job 9:11), just after the verse about walking on the sea. Most commentators now read the verse as a revelation of God's glory, not a plan to leave them.
r: Exodus 33:19–22; Exodus 34:6; 1 Kings 19:11; Job 9:8; Job 9:11; Amos 7:8

p: Phantasma: an apparition. Sailors' tales of ghosts on the water were common.
b: Phantasma means something that appears, an apparition or ghost. The disciples' fear is natural: a figure on the water before dawn. The same word is in Matthew 14:26. Later Christians used the passage against the Docetists, who taught that Jesus only seemed to have a body: the disciples thought he was a phantom, and they were wrong.

p: Egō eimi can mean "It's me." It is also the way God names himself.
b: In ordinary Greek egō eimi means "It is I" or "It's me." But in the Greek Old Testament it is how God speaks of himself: egō eimi ho ōn, "I am the one who is" (Exodus 3:14 in Greek), and egō eimi, "I am," in Isaiah's great sayings (Isaiah 41:4; Isaiah 43:10; Isaiah 51:12, where the Greek doubles it: "I am, I am the one who comforts you"). Coming right after walking on the sea and "passing by," many scholars hear the divine name. Others think Mark means only that Jesus identified himself. The site keeps "I am" so the reader can hear both. Jesus uses the words again before the high priest (14:62).
r: 13:6; 14:62; Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 41:4; Isaiah 43:10; Isaiah 51:12; Matthew 14:27; John 6:20; John 8:58

p: Mark ties the walk on the water to the loaves. Interpreters ask what the disciples should have understood.
b: Mark explains their astonishment at the sea by their failure about the bread, though the two events seem unconnected. Readings: the feeding showed that Jesus does what only God does, feeding his people in the wilderness, so they should not be surprised that he also does what God does on the sea; or the feeding should have shown them that he would care for them; or the loaves point ahead to the Lord's Supper and his death, which they cannot yet grasp. Jesus himself presses the point in 8:14–21.

p: The disciples' hearts are "hardened," the word Mark used of Jesus' opponents (3:5). Matthew has them worship instead.
b: Pōroō means to harden, to make callous. Mark used the noun for the hardness of heart of those who watched Jesus on the Sabbath (3:5), and Jesus will ask the disciples, "Have your hearts turned hard?" (8:17). This is Mark's bluntest statement about the Twelve. Matthew 14:33 ends the same scene with the disciples bowing down and saying, "You really are God's Son." Mark's readers are left to ask whether they too have missed what the loaves meant.

p: A fertile plain on the northwest shore of the lake, between Capernaum and Magdala.
b: The plain of Gennesaret (Ginosar) is a small, well-watered plain on the west shore, between Capernaum and Magdala. Josephus praises its fertility and mild climate, saying walnuts, palms, figs and olives all grew there together (Jewish War 3.516–521). The lake itself was sometimes called the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1). The first-century boat found in 1986 came out of the mud here.

p: Kraspedon is the tassel Jewish men wore on the corners of their cloaks (Numbers 15:38), not a "hem."
b: The kraspedon is the tassel, Hebrew tsitsit, that the law commands on the four corners of a garment, with a blue cord, to remind Israel of God's commands (Numbers 15:37–41; Deuteronomy 22:12). Older English Bibles said "hem" or "border." That Jesus wore tassels shows him as an observant Jew. Touching the tassel was perhaps touching the sign of God's commands on a holy man. See 5:27.

a: everyone who touched him was saved
p: The same verb, sōzō, as the woman's healing (5:28, 34). Mark ends the chapter with crowds who believe the touch heals.
b: Mark closes with a summary: whole districts carry their sick to wherever Jesus is, and all who touch him are "saved," healed and made whole (see 5:34). The contrast with Nazareth (6:5–6) is sharp: there unbelief blocked his power; here eager trust receives it. Matthew 14:36 has the stronger compound verb, "made completely well."
